nutshell: Tampa Bay's folk scene is broad, older-skewing and strongly seasonal, and its deepest roots are immigrant rather than Anglo. Tarpon Springs' Kalymnian Greeks have kept island violin, laouto and circle dancing alive since the 1905 sponge-diver migration: the first fiddler ever recorded inside the metro (WPA, 1939-40) was a Greek island violinist, and both of the MSA's NEA Heritage Fellows are Tarpon Greeks. Dunedin turned a 1957 gift of school bagpipes into a world-champion pipe band. Ybor City's 1880s cigar-worker clubs still stand, but their music has mostly gone; Puerto Rican bomba, Cuban dance classes and Caribbean carnival carry the Latin side now. For a fiddler the weekly reality is about 26 bluegrass and 13 old-time jams a month, many held in daylight at senior centers, libraries and breweries; one host's Sunday circuit of four Irish sessions; and two contras. There is no folk society, but WMNF radio (1979), the Will McLean Foundation's festival ranch and house concerts hold the song scene together. Everything swells from November to April.

timeline.event: Fort Brooke established (Jan 10) at the mouth of the Hillsborough River to watch the Seminoles under the Treaty of Moultrie Creek; later HQ of the Second Seminole War (1835-42). No documentation of Tocobaga or Seminole-era music in the area was found.
1880s: John K. Cheyney starts Tarpon Springs' sponge business; Key West and Bahamian sponge hookers settle there (the Black/Bahamian community Billy 'the Kid' Emerson later grew up in).
Vicente Martinez-Ybor moves his cigar factory from Key West and founds Ybor City; Tampa annexes it in 1887.
Centro Espanol, Ybor's first mutual-aid society, founded; the clubs' dances, picnics and theaters become the neighborhood's music infrastructure.
Jose Marti speaks from the steps of Ybor's factory, a speech said to have led directly to war.
L'Unione Italiana (Italian Club) founded with 107 members (3,000+ by 1935); its building had a dance floor and theater.
El Club Nacional Cubano founded Oct 10 (renamed El Circulo Cubano 1902). Same year Dunedin, named by Scots J.O. Douglas and James Somerville after Dun Eideann (Edinburgh), incorporates as a town.
Dunedin, named by Scots J.O. Douglas and James Somerville after Dùn Èideann (Edinburgh), is incorporated as a town.
Afro-Cuban La Union Marti-Maceo founded; Centro Asturiano (Apr 8) and Circulo Cubano follow in 1902.
Centro Asturiano de Tampa founded by 546 Asturian immigrants; its 1914 theater became famous for zarzuela (Spain's El Arte de Teatro sent a full-time correspondent) and hosted Ernesto Lecuona.
South Florida Fair founded in downtown Tampa (named Florida State Fair from 1915).
John Cocoris brings Greek helmet divers to Tarpon Springs; Dodecanese islanders (Kalymnos, Symi, Halki) soon dominate, bringing violin-laouto island dance music.
St. Nicholas Greek Orthodox parish founded; numbering of the Epiphany (100th in 2006) implies a first celebration c.1907.
Circulo Cubano's present building opens (theater, ballroom, cantina) after fire destroyed the first.
December: the Tin Can Tourists, America's first RV club, founded by about 20 auto-campers at DeSoto Park, Tampa; new members were inducted with a chorus of 'The More We Get Together', the club song.

Masaryktown (Hernando County) founded by Czechoslovak colonists (60 of 61 founders Slovak); Mirror Lake Shuffleboard Club founded in St. Petersburg (it later held dances), emblem of the retiree winter culture.
Tampa Red (Hudson Whittaker), raised in Tampa where he learned from his brother Eddie and street musician 'Piccolo Pete', is in Chicago by 1925 and takes the city's name.
1927-28: Zora Neale Hurston collects songs and tales at the Everglades Cypress Lumber Co. camp, Loughman, Polk County (outside the MSA), material for Mules and Men (1935).
Plant City Lions Club holds the first Florida Strawberry Festival (paused for WWII, revived 1948 by American Legion Post 26).

April: the Brooksville PTA announces a county old-time fiddlers' contest, urging fiddlers to 'tune up their instruments and get the stiffness out of their fingers'; small admission fee, prize for best fiddler in Hernando County.
West Tampa's Charlie Brantley starts his career with the Florida Collegians, a group of Tampa musicians.
August: Joe Budowiski of the Nobleton/Stafford area (Hernando) wins first prize at a fiddlers' contest in Lake City, per the Brooksville Sun's community column.

June 21: Herbert Halpert's WPA/Library of Congress Southern States expedition records the house band at the Cuban Club, Ybor City (punto guajiro, guabina, 'Five Cuban Drum Rhythms': son, rumba, bembe, conga, mani).
Aug 23-27: Stetson Kennedy and Robert Cook record Spanish, Cuban and Italian songs, lullabies, tales and riddles in Ybor City for the Florida Folklore Recording Expedition.

Aug 25-28: Greek songs recorded in Tarpon Springs (Alton Morris interviewing, Kennedy and Cook recording), with violinist Louis Peronis, santouri player Harry Perris and mandola player George Kafezio; Aug 28 Morris records Slovak singers at Masaryktown.

May 12: John Filareton records the Philoptochos Society program in Tarpon Springs: Halki sousta, Kalymnos dance, pentozali, kalamatianos, syrtos on violin (Peronis), laouto (George Kaletizis) and santouri (Perris).

July: the WPA's only cracker fiddle recordings in this part of Florida are made outside the MSA, in Kenansville (Osceola) and Sebring (Highlands): G. G. Albritton's 'Collier in the Scrub' with fiddlesticks ('straws').
April: 'Folksongs and Folklore of Ybor City', a Federal Writers' Project typescript by Wayne A. Blossom (play songs, cradle songs, superstitions), now digitized from UF's P.K. Yonge Library.
Current St. Nicholas Cathedral consecrated at Epiphany by Archbishop Athenagoras.
Charlie Brantley forms Charlie Brantley and His Original Honey Dippers, the leading Black R&B band in Tampa through the late 1940s.
Ray Charles moves to Tampa; Ybor's Fiesta Day begins (inferred from 80th in 2027); red tide wipes out the Gulf sponge beds.

Ray Charles moves to Tampa (fall 1946 per Tampa Bay Music History; 1947 per Wikipedia), boards with the Brantleys at 1901 Cherry St, plays piano with the Honey Dippers and, per a 1991 Orlando Sentinel headline, 'wound up yodeling with a country and western band in Tampa'.
First documented Pasco County Fair, Dade City (Jan 20-24); the Florida Strawberry Festival resumes.

Tom Reese returns to Pinellas Park and turns the 1911 Royal Palm Hotel into the Contemporary Arts Gallery; when the art school fails he starts poetry readings and folksingers' nights (renamed Beaux Arts 1962).
Polish American Society of St. Petersburg and German-American Society of Pinellas founded.
First Florida Folk Festival at White Springs (outside the MSA), which Alton C. Morris persuaded the Florida women's music clubs to stage; it becomes the scene's statewide anchor.
Dunedin Highland Junior High opens; a gift set of bagpipes from Scotland via newspaper owner Roy Thomson and piper Matt Forsythe start Dunedin's school pipe bands.

Dade City's Dr. Edward L. 'Doc' Flemming Jr. begins two decades (1960-81) as a Florida Folk Festival participant and promoter; with Thelma Boltin he creates the Heart of Florida Folk Festival in Dade City (year not found).

Jim Morrison, a St. Petersburg Junior College student, reads poetry at Reese's coffeehouse with his back to the audience; Fred Neil, Vince Martin, Gamble Rogers, Will McLean and fiddler Bobby Hicks also pass through in the 1960s.

Contemporary Arts Gallery renamed the Beaux Arts Gallery; Fred Neil, Vince Martin, Jerry Jeff Walker, Gamble Rogers, Will McLean and Bobby Hicks pass through in the 1960s; Jack Kerouac is thrown out for drinking (mid-1960s).
City of Dunedin Pipe Band founded; Stirling, Scotland becomes Dunedin's sister city (June 15).
Dunedin Highland Games & Festival Committee formed to fund the city and school pipe bands.
Tsabouna (island bagpipe) player Nikitas Tsimouris emigrates from Kalymnos to Tarpon Springs.
Members of Tampa's Hillsborough Sertoma Club conceive the Sertoma Youth Ranch near Brooksville, later home to the area's bluegrass festivals.
The Cotton Club, last business in Tampa's historically Black Central Avenue district (a Chitlin' Circuit stop), closes amid unrest and interstate construction.
St. Petersburg International Folk Fair Society (SPIFFS) founded; its International Folk Fair reaches its 51st edition in March 2027 (Pinellas Park).
Jim Strickland ('Mr. Ethnic') takes a banjo class from 'Cousin' Ernie Williams and starts playing old-time (Hyde Park Hysterical Society String Band, Wednesday Night Fiddle Support Group).
Fire destroys the uninsured Beaux Arts music room; a bigger fire about 12 years later wrecks the upper floors.
Sertoma Spring Bluegrass Festival founded, later called 'the oldest bluegrass festival in the southeast'.
Cracker Country living-history museum founded at the Florida State Fairgrounds.
John Lulias founds the Levendia Greek dance troupe.

Florida Folklife Program established by the legislature; WMNF signs on Sept 14 with folk/acoustic mornings and bluegrass drive-time; John Lulias founds the Levendia Greek dance troupe in Tarpon Springs.
WMNF's Celtic show Music of the Isles begins ('since 1979').

Strickland starts old-time programming on WMNF; Skipper's Smokehouse opens; the Fort Brooke cemetery is rediscovered under a downtown garage site, leading to the 1981 Seminole reburial and the Seminole Tribe's Tampa Reservation.
Skipper's Smokehouse opens at 910 Skipper Rd; Jeannie Holton starts on WMNF (Feb); The Jewish Sound (later Sunday Simcha) begins.

Bill Dudley forms the Wind That Shakes the Barley, called Florida's first Irish traditional band; Strickland begins old-time programming on WMNF; the Scottish American Society of Dunedin is founded and Scottish country dancing begins there.
Wat Mongkolratanaram established; Tampa Greek Festival begins.
First Florida State Fiddlers convention and contest (Santa Fe High School, Alachua; outside the MSA); a 1989 bill makes it the official state contest.
First WMNF Tropical Heatwave at the Cuban Club, Ybor City.
Florida Old Time Music Championship begins at the Pioneer Florida Museum, Dade City; Sandy Keith becomes Dunedin's piping director.
First Guavaween in Ybor; first Tampa Bay apprenticeship in tsambouna (Tsimouris).
Sacred steel pioneer Willie Eason settles in St. Petersburg.
Tampa Bay History Center founded; Tsimouris receives the Florida Folk Heritage Award.

Will McLean ('Florida's Black Hat Troubadour') dies in January; the Will McLean Foundation is established; Michael Woolfe of New Port Richey and Aubrey Haney of Brandon place at the state fiddle contest; Donegal fiddler Edward J. Keeney retires to Florida.
Nikitas Tsimouris named an NEA National Heritage Fellow.
Florida Folklife's Bob Stone finds steel guitars in House of God churches in the St. Petersburg area, the start of the 'Sacred Steel' documentation (Arhoolie album 1997).
Tampa Friends of Old-Time Dance incorporated (Mar 22); the Cuban Club building faces foreclosure.
Pinellas Park buys the Beaux Arts property for $162,000 and razes it.
Tampa Bay Blues Festival begins at Vinoy Park.
Dunedin Scottish Country Dancers formally organized.
Sid Flannery joins WMNF's Saturday Bluegrass Show; Sacred Grounds Coffee House's ~20-year run on Fowler Ave begins around this time (inferred from 'closing two years ago' in 2018 and a 20-year run).
State Sen. John Grant zeroes $104,000 of WMNF's state funding over Iris DeMent's 'Wasteland of the Free'; listeners give $122,000 in a day and a half.
Summerside, Prince Edward Island, becomes Dunedin's second sister city.
Skipper's wins 'Best Blues Club in America'. Florida Folk Show begins around this time (inferred from '25 years on public radio' in 2026).
Ian Malinowski of Tarpon Springs wins the Rustic (old-time) division of the Florida State Fiddle Contest after a decade of placings.
Helmet maker Nicholas Toth named an NEA National Heritage Fellow; Tampa Bay Steel Orchestra formed.
Earliest Florida Snow Ball contra weekend in the online archive.
Irish session at Bridie Gannon's, Tarpon Springs, ends after the pub's new owner installs dartboards and jukeboxes.
100th Epiphany, attended by Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew; first Tampa Bay Caribbean Carnival (inferred).
First-Sunday Four Green Fields session listed on thesession (it ran until the Platt St pub closed in Dec 2020).
Bomba Body Dance & Drumming Co. / CuKiAra founded.
Creative Clay's first Folkfest St. Pete on Central Avenue.
Folklorist Tina Bucuvalas becomes Tarpon Springs' Curator of Arts and Historical Resources; the city's Center for Gulf Coast Folklife runs workshops in bouzouki and violin.
Hideaway Cafe opens at 1756 Central Ave, St. Pete; Ella's Americana Folk Art Cafe opens in Seminole Heights (15 years before its 2024 close).
Night in the Islands begins: Greek music and social dancing on the Sponge Docks monthly April-October.
Iain Donaldson succeeds Sandy Keith as Dunedin's band director.
NEA grants $40,000 to Tarpon Springs' Center for Gulf Coast Folklife.
Molly Malone's (Davis Islands) session begins.
David Hosler retires from Taylor Guitars and opens Seven C Music in St. Petersburg.
Original FOTMC ends after 33 years; the Highland Games committee becomes the Dunedin Scottish Arts Foundation.
Sacred Grounds Coffee House in Tampa closes (approximately).
Trailside Jammers old-time jam starts on the Pinellas Trail, Dunedin (about 2017).
City of Dunedin Pipe Band wins the World Pipe Band Championships in Grade 2 and is promoted to Grade 1, then the only US Grade 1 band.
Paddy League's Kalymnian music and oral poetry apprenticeship with two Tarpon Springs apprentices.
City of Dunedin wins the Grade 1 North American Championship at Maxville, the first American winner since the 1960s.
COVID: Skipper's Smokehouse announces its closing after 40 years (final show Sept 27); it reopens in 2021.
Four Green Fields' Platt Street pub (and its session) closes; the 2nd-Sunday session at the Irish Pub on 4th starts in August.
Jan 6: Tarpon Springs' Epiphany is held without public spectators; the procession is limited to clergy, dignitaries and cross divers and the blessing is livestreamed.
Skipper's reopens as 'Skipper's 2.0' (soft opening July 8).
Florida Snow Ball cancelled for COVID; the Strandhill Public House (Brandon) session goes on 'hiatus' and does not return.
Hideaway Cafe's final show (Apr 30) after its lease was not renewed; Hideaway Cafe Presents goes roving; Will McLean Foundation takes over Sertoma Youth Ranch as Florida Sand Music Ranch.
Sertoma Youth Ranch becomes Florida Sand Music Ranch under the Will McLean Foundation; FOTMC Inc. founded; Suncoast United Pipes & Drums organized.
William 'Billy the Kid' Emerson, Sun Records songwriter turned Tarpon Springs pastor, dies.
Four Green Fields ends Irish sessions at all its pubs (August), 'after decades'.
Hurricane Milton cancels the Tampa Greek Festival; the Polish American Society reopens after storm repairs; first Tampa Haitian Flag Day.

Nov 20: anthropologists' excursion to Tarpon Springs with Tina Bucuvalas, bouzouki teacher Leonidas Zafiris and Levendia's Maria Kouskoutis, evidence the Greek music and dance teaching chain is intact.
First Central Florida all-day Sacred Harp singing (Jan 13, Orlando); Ella's Americana Folk Art Cafe closes Sept 1.
Flanagan's (Dunedin) 4th-Sunday session begins (September); hurricanes close McArthur's Irish Pub, which reopens in 2025 as the Irish Pub on Fourth.
The five legacy Ybor clubs hold a joint Piquiniqui for Ybor's 140th (Dec 14); 10th Festival de Bomba y Plena.
Wednesday Writers Room songwriting collective forms (January); Sunday Sampler Tampa launches at New World; Good Folk Fest revives Folkfest at the Coliseum (Nov 16).
Tampa Bay Old Time Jam starts monthly in Bradenton (Manatee County).
120th Epiphany cross dive (Jan 6), won by Athos Karistinos.

Will McLean Music Festival held in March at Florida Sand Music Ranch (80 groups, 3 stages, an Old Time Gathering); 2027 dates set for Mar 12-14. The Center for Gulf Coast Folklife page disappears from tarponarts.org (404 by October).
Neon Lunchbox (in the former Hideaway space) closes Aug 29; the 1923 building is listed for $3.6 million in October. Old Time Sailors shanty show for 813 Day is cancelled.
The 4th-Sunday contra moves from the Gulfport Casino to the Town Apartments North rec center; Snow Ball moves to the Boca Ciega High School gym; Irish Pub on 4th session revived (September).

Coastal Lifestyle House Concerts in Dunedin ask a $25 donation, all to the artist (https://undiscovered.music/venues/coastal_lifestyle_house_concerts). Will McLean Sunday Sampler $15 advance / $20 door (https://www.willmclean.com/sunday-sampler-tampa); Palladium songwriter-in-the-round $20-50. Cuban dance class $20 drop-in (https://www.yusnielgarcia.com/). Thanksgiving Bluegrass Festival $21.50-$154 (https://evansmediasource.com/events/); McLean festival camping $20-40 a night (https://www.willmclean.com/music-festival/festival-tickets-fees-camping).

surprises: The first fiddler ever recorded inside today's Tampa Bay MSA was a Greek island violinist, not a cracker: in 1939-40 WPA crews recorded Louis Peronis (violin) with laouto and santouri playing a Halki sousta and a Kalymnos circle dance in Tarpon Springs. The cracker fiddlers were recorded outside the metro in Sebring, and Pasco County has zero items in the collection (https://www.loc.gov/item/flwpa000334/, https://www.loc.gov/item/flwpa000381/).

A 1957 gift set of bagpipes for a new junior high school, arranged through newspaper owner Roy Thomson, grew into the City of Dunedin Pipe Band, which won the 2018 Grade 2 World Championship and in 2019 the Grade 1 North American title at Maxville, after the 78th Fraser Highlanders had first been wrongly announced as winners (https://www.dunedinsafoundation.com/history/, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Dunedin_Pipe_Band_(United_States)).

Dunedin's pipe major, Iain Donaldson, is also the city's Director of Piping, directs both school pipe bands, and with his wife runs the bagpipe shop on Main Street, a family firm founded in 1965 as The British Shop in Buffalo, NY (https://www.dunedinsafoundation.com/about/, https://www.lothianbagpipesupplies.com/).

A metro of 3.4 million has one Irish session host and no weeknight Irish session: Jessica Conlan runs all three pubs' sessions (1st-4th Sundays, all at 5pm) (https://thesession.org/sessions/3444, https://thesession.org/sessions/9004).

Every Irish session that died here was killed by a pub owner, not a lack of players. Bridie Gannon's (2005) replaced the musicians with 'electronic dart boards, jukeboxes'; Four Green Fields, opened in 1992 as 'the country's only authentic thatched roof Irish pub', cut sessions at all its pubs in Aug 2023 'after decades' (https://thesession.org/sessions/1055, https://thesession.org/sessions/6499).

Jams by daylight: old-timers play Wednesdays 11am under an oak on the Pinellas Trail sidewalk in Dunedin; the Thonotosassa bluegrass jam moved to the park gazebo on Oct 31, 2026 ('BRING A CHAIR'); and the Elfers Senior Center Wednesday jam has run 'more than 30 years' with a free lunch for registered players 60+ (https://www.tampabay.com/photos/2025/02/23/trailside-jammers-pinellas-trail-dunedin-old-time-music/, https://jaminfo.otddi.com/, https://www.tampabay.com/photos/2026/10/23/pasco-county-elfers-senior-center-music-jam/).

The fiddler at a Tampa contra may be Kathie Aagaard, retired assistant principal violist of The Florida Orchestra, who plays Hardanger fiddle and was in the Wind That Shakes the Barley, called Florida's first Irish traditional band, when Bill Dudley founded it in 1980. Both still play TFOOTD dances (https://www.floridamemory.com/items/show/237026, https://tampabaycontra.com/home/bands_callers/).

Jim Morrison's first stage was a Pinellas Park folk coffeehouse: around 1961 he read poetry there with his back to the audience. The owner, Tom Reese, banned alcohol so firmly that he threw Jack Kerouac out for drinking from a flask (https://stpetecatalyst.com/vintage-st-pete-tom-reese-and-the-beaux-arts-gallery/).

There is a Sacred Harp singing inside the Florida State Fair: a Cooper-book singing each February in the Cracker Country living-history village. The metro's other regular singing is a rural Primitive Baptist church on the Hillsborough-Polk line that sings the Cooper book on fifth Sundays (https://shapenotesingings.com/singings/florida-state-fair-singing, https://shapenotesingings.com/singings/bethlehem-pbc-5th-sunday-singing).

Sacred steel was 'discovered' by outsiders in St. Petersburg: in 1992 Florida Folklife folklorist Bob Stone found House of God churches in the St. Pete area using steel guitars in worship, which led to Arhoolie's Sacred Steel series. Pioneer Willie Eason lived in St. Pete from 1986 until his death there in 2005 (https://archive.arhoolie.org/collections/robert-stone-sacred-steel-collection).

Florida's old-time championship was born in rural Pasco: it ran 33 years (1982-2015) at the Pioneer Florida Museum in Dade City, started after Dade City banjoist Ernie Williams won at the Athens, Alabama fiddlers' convention. Its revival (2022) is 150 miles away in White Springs (https://www.fotmcinc.com/our-story).

The region's festival grounds began as a youth ranch dreamed up in 1973 by three Tampa Sertoma Club members (a state policeman, an insurance agent and an auto-parts store owner). Since 2022 the 80 acres belong to the Will McLean Foundation, named for a Florida folksinger, and host 15+ festivals a year (https://floridasandmusicranch.com/about/, https://www.willmclean.com/will-mclean-foundation/about-the-foundation).

A Donegal fiddler from the kitchen where John Doherty played, Edward J. Keeney (1922-2009), retired to the Tampa Bay area, won a 1999 Florida Folk Heritage Award and taught state-funded Irish fiddle apprenticeships (https://donegalfiddlemusic.ie/edward-keeney-1922-2009/, https://dos.fl.gov/cultural/programs/florida-folklife-program/folk-heritage-awards/list-of-past-recipients/edward-j-keeney/).

Sun Records songwriter Billy 'the Kid' Emerson ('Red Hot') grew up in Tarpon Springs in a Bahamian family that hooked sponges before the Greeks came; he sailed on sponge schooners at eight and his mother spoke Greek (https://dos.fl.gov/cultural/programs/florida-folklife-program/folk-heritage-awards/list-of-past-recipients/william-emerson/).

Dunedin's second sister city is Summerside, Prince Edward Island, the Blue Jays have trained there since 1977, and a Newfoundland and Labrador Society of Florida claims about 1,100 members, yet no Cape Breton, Maritime or Quebecois fiddle session could be found anywhere in the MSA (https://www.dunedin.gov/Community/Arts-Culture/Scottish-History-of-Dunedin, https://www.facebook.com/groups/2009674299347582/photos/).
The best-documented 'Tampa Bay Old Time Jam' isn't in the Tampa Bay MSA: it meets in Bradenton (https://www.jamfinder.org/jams/bradenton-tampa-bay-old-time-jam/).

Modern western square dancing beats contra about eight to one: roughly 8 clubs and 16 dances a month against TFOOTD's 2 contras. Plant City's Strawberry Square, 'the square dance capital of the South', has a floating hardwood floor inside a residential park whose website also handles lot sales and background checks (http://www.dancergram.com/a-00-WestCoastClubsLink.html, https://www.strawberrysquaredancing.com/).
In 1997 a state senator zeroed WMNF's $104,000 state grant over Iris DeMent's 'Wasteland of the Free'; listeners raised $122,000 in a day and a half (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WMNF).

In 2014 the Tampa Bay Rays brought Seminole medicine man Bobby Henry (Florida Folk Heritage Award 2001) to Tropicana Field as a 'rainmaker' to end a losing streak (https://www.tampabay.com/archive/2014/06/10/medicine-man/).

In a maritime metro full of pirate festivals, no shanty sing could be found, and the one shanty band booked for 813 Day 2026 cancelled because it had 'lost their compass and are lost at sea' (https://www.cltampa.com/arts/tampas-813-day-celebrations-include-a-concert-from-giant-sea-shanty-ensemble/).
curiosities: Tampa Bay has about 4 Irish sessions a month, all on Sunday at 5pm and all run by one host. How does Irish-sessions-per-million compare across the 20 metros, and how many metros depend on a single organizer for an entire tradition?

How seasonal are folk calendars in snowbird metros? Compare January vs July event counts for Tampa, Orlando, Phoenix and Riverside against a non-seasonal metro such as Seattle or Minneapolis (here Scottish country dance, polka, house concerts and gospel tours all run roughly Nov-Apr).

Modern western square dancing outnumbers contra about 8 to 1 here. Is that ratio typical of retirement-heavy metros (Phoenix, Orlando, Riverside), and the reverse of college-heavy metros (Boston, Seattle, San Francisco)?

What share of each metro's jams meet before 5pm? Tampa's old-time and bluegrass life runs largely on weekday mornings at senior centers, libraries and churches. Is that a Florida pattern or a retiree pattern?

Is any other metro's earliest recorded fiddle non-Anglo? Tampa's is Dodecanese Greek (1939-40). Compare Detroit's Polish, Minneapolis's Scandinavian, Houston's Czech and Chicago's Irish fiddlers in the LOC record.

How often do pub sessions die by owner decision rather than lack of players? Tampa lost Bridie Gannon's (2005), James Joyce (2013), Strandhill (2021) and three Four Green Fields sessions (2020-23). Compare session lifespans on thesession.org across metros.

Why do fast-growing Sun Belt metros (Tampa, Orlando, Phoenix, Dallas, Riverside) seem to lack membership folk societies while smaller northern metros have them? Do in-migrants keep their loyalty to clubs 'back home'?

Where do the Canadian snowbirds play? A 1,100-member Newfoundland society, a PEI sister city and a Blue Jays camp produce no findable Maritime sessions here. Do kitchen parties happen privately in mobile-home parks, and does Phoenix-Mesa show the same invisibility?
How many Cooper-book (vs Denson) Sacred Harp singings sit inside the 20 largest MSAs? Tampa's is a rural Primitive Baptist church plus a State Fair singing; is that unique among big metros?

Is Dunedin's three-tier public-school bagpipe pipeline (middle school, high school, Grade 1 city band) unique in the US, and why does 'the Scotland of Florida' have elite pipers but no Scottish fiddle club? Do other Highland Games towns support Scottish fiddling?
Which metros have community-radio folk hosts as long-serving as WMNF's (Ed Lehmann 1979, Jeannie Holton 1980, Bill Dudley's Celtic show 1980)? Compare KBOO, WFMU, KPFA, KUOW and WFHB.

Why did Ybor City's Spanish, Cuban and Italian clubs survive as buildings but lose their orchestras and dance ensembles, when Key West's San Carlos Institute or New York's Spanish Benevolent Society kept some performing life? When did the last resident club orchestra play?

State folk honors per capita: about 20 of 143 Florida Folk Heritage Awards have Tampa Bay ties, nine from Tarpon Springs (pop. ~25,000) alone. How do other states' heritage awards distribute across their big metros, and why do small diaspora towns dominate?

Florida's folk-song institutions (Will McLean festival, Best New Florida Song contest) insist on songs about the state itself. Do other metros have a comparable state-identity songwriting movement (Kerrville in Texas, Woody Guthrie events in Oklahoma), and does it make their scenes songwriter-led rather than tradition-led?

Large Mexican and Puerto Rican farmworker communities in Wimauma, Ruskin and Plant City show no online son jarocho, folklorico or jibaro music. Is that absence real or an artifact of WhatsApp/church organizing, and how does it compare with Texas and California metros?
In which metros does old-time live in the exurban edge rather than the core? Here it is east Pasco (Dade City, San Antonio) and a Dunedin sidewalk, while Tampa proper has almost none.

COUNTS: recurring_events lists 65 in-MSA events (plus 3 just outside, flagged). Headline totals count 58 of them; 7 are kept but flagged count_in_totals:false: three non-participatory items (City of Dunedin Pipe Band rehearsals, Piper on the Pier, restaurant Greek music) and four jams with no dated 2024-26 evidence (Dunedin Dulcimers, Snellgrove's, Leaven slow jam, Soggy Bottom). SEASONALITY: per_month is the in-season rate; seasonal events carry a 'seasonal' field and a per_month_annual_avg (Scottish country dance and polka Nov-Apr, house concerts Sep/Oct-Apr, Sunday Sampler Nov-May); the 12-month average total is about 139 vs 143 in season. Annual events (Epiphany, festivals, State Fair singing) are included at 0.083/month. No headcounts exist to show how much bigger jams get in winter. OPEN MICS: the folk_open_mic events (about 39/month) are a curated subset of the folk-leaning entries on one volunteer list that shows about 60 open mics and 37 open jams a week, mostly bar/rock, Pinellas-centric and partly stale; excluding open mics the total is about 104/month. DISTINCT TRADITIONS: the computed free-text count (76) was replaced by a hand count of 24 traditions with dated 2024-26 practice in the MSA: Irish session, old-time, bluegrass, contra, modern western square/round, clogging (federation list only), Scottish country dance, Highland piping/drumming and dance, Irish step dance, international folk dance, Israeli dance, Sacred Harp, folk song/singer-songwriter, Greek (Dodecanese music and parish dance), Polish polka, German club dance, Puerto Rican bomba/plena, Cuban dance, Mexican folklorico, Caribbean carnival/steel pan, Haitian, Filipino, Indian classical, Colombian. Excluded: sacred steel (no current congregation verified), Serbian dance (undated), Southern gospel (presented concerts), klezmer (radio only), English country dance (only at one annual weekend), Seminole, Bahamian, Ybor club culture. NOT FOUND (not proof of absence): Comhaltas branch, céilí/set dance, Cape Breton/Maritime/Quebecois sessions, Scottish fiddle club, morris/sword, standing ECD series, shanty sing, folk society, son jarocho, joropo, Bosnian sevdah, Vietnamese music, powwow, a current tsambouna player, tunes named for the area. CONFLICTS: Polish American Society polka dances Sunday (Facebook) vs Saturday (2025-26 schedule mapping); Will McLean festival founded 1990, 1991 or 1992 and placed in Brooksville or Dade City; Epiphany numbering implies c.1907 vs the usual 1903/1906; Dunedin Highland Games 1966 vs committee 1967; Bethlehem PBC address Lithia vs Mulberry (counted inside the MSA by ZIP and OSM); state fiddle contest's first venue (Alachua per FSFA vs White Springs); Nicholas Toth NEA 2003 (arts.gov) vs 2004 (state); Stetson Kennedy FHA 1988 vs 1998; WMNF's Celtic show Music of the Isles is on the HD4 subchannel, not the main schedule, and Mr. Ethnic's old-time show has no playlist newer than 2017. The Sertoma/EMS spring bluegrass festival is marked hiatus because no 2026 edition was found. The Irish Pub on 4th session revival rests on one Sept 2026 host comment; the Tuesday Tampa Jam may have moved to Wednesdays.
